analysis.one_liner: Lets the government strip monopoly protections from brand-name drugs priced higher than in five other countries.
analysis.headline: Six senators backed the bill, but it never got a hearing or a vote and died in committee when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Health and Human Services Department to review the price of every brand-name drug each year against prices in Canada, the United Kingdom, Germany, France, and Japan. Any drug priced above the median of those countries would be declared "excessively priced," and the government would then void its monopoly protections and license any company to make cheaper generic or biosimilar versions, with the brand-name maker paid a royalty. The bill was introduced by Senator Bernie Sanders with six Democratic cosponsors in January 2019 and was sent to the Senate Health Committee, which never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who take brand-name prescription drugs in the United States, where drug prices run far above what the same drugs cost in other wealthy countries. Anyone whose insurer, employer, or government program pays for those drugs also benefits indirectly, since lower drug prices flow into lower premiums and lower public spending.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Americans who take brand-name prescription drugs

how_it_helps.text: Requires annual review of all brand-name drugs against the median price in Canada, the UK, Germany, France, and Japan; any drug priced above that median is deemed excessively priced [S2] [S3].

For drugs found excessively priced, the bill voids government-granted exclusivity, issues open licenses so any company can make the drug, and speeds up review of generic and biosimilar applications within 8 months [S2] [S3].
Licensed copies must be sold below the price the government found excessive, and the brand-name maker keeps a reasonable royalty rather than losing the patent outright [S3].

Manufacturers must report prices, revenues, research spending, and advertising spending for each brand-name drug annually, with penalties for late or false reports, creating public visibility into how drugs are priced [S2] [S3].
Any person can petition the Secretary for an excessive-price review of a specific drug, with the results posted on a public database [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, which would lose monopoly revenue on any drug the government found overpriced. Industry groups would also lose a bargaining chip in price negotiations, since the threat of losing exclusivity would hang over every brand-name price. Some portion of lower drug revenue could mean less industry-funded research, though the bill preserves royalties for patent holders.

drawbacks.text: The bill uses prices in five other countries as the benchmark, but those countries use government price controls of their own; a company could argue the comparison understates what it actually costs to develop new medicines [S3].

Voiding exclusivity and licensing production when a price is deemed excessive is a major intervention in the patent system, and manufacturers would likely challenge it in court, creating years of uncertainty about whether it could actually be carried out [S3].

If lower prices cut into what brand-name companies can recoup on drugs that do make money, some risky research on new medicines might get less funding, a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit to patients is large: American brand-name drug prices are among the highest in the world, and the bill attacks the mechanism that keeps them high — exclusive rights granted by the government. The main real cost is to the brand-name industry's revenue and possibly to the pace of some new-drug development, and the royalty structure mitigates rather than eliminates that. The design is aggressive but not confiscatory, since patent holders keep royalty income. The drawback is that no Congress came close to testing whether it could survive industry lawsuits.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never held a hearing or vote, and the bill expired when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Sanders introduced the bill on January 10, 2019, with five Democratic colleagues joining as cosponsors [S1] [S3] [S4].
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S5].
That is the last action the bill ever received; no committee markup, no hearing, no floor vote, and no further action is recorded before the Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers are better off because the bill never advanced, since they keep their exclusive rights and pricing power over drugs sold in the United States. Patients paying high drug prices gained nothing from the bill's death.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the sponsor was an Independent and all six cosponsors were Democrats, with no Republican support recorded, but the partisan shape of a floor vote was never tested [S4].

industries.note: The bill would strip exclusive rights and license generic competition for any drug priced above the median of five peer countries, directly threatening the pricing power that makes U.S. drug prices among the world's highest. Its interest in the bill ran squarely against patients' interest in lower prices.

The bill would grant open licenses letting any company make licensed drugs and would speed up review of their applications, creating new market openings. Cheaper copies are exactly what lowers costs for patients.

Manufacturers would have to disclose annual marketing and advertising spending per drug, adding public scrutiny of spending that drives U.S. prices up. The disclosure itself is the cost; the public interest is in seeing it.
